questions.stem: The Great Famine of 1845–1852 drove large-scale emigration from Ireland, including to the Australian colonies. Its immediate cause was:
options: the eviction of tenants to make way for railways
a cholera epidemic that closed the Irish ports
the repeated failure of the potato crop through blight
the collapse of the Irish linen trade after free trade
questions.explanation: Potato blight destroyed the staple food of the Irish rural poor in successive years, causing mass starvation, disease and emigration. Evictions did follow, but they were a consequence of the famine rather than its cause.

questions.stem: Edward Gibbon Wakefield's idea of 'systematic colonisation' shaped assisted migration to colonies such as South Australia. Under this approach, the passages of free emigrants were to be funded mainly by:
options: a tax on convict labour hired by pastoralists
donations collected by British parish charities
fees paid by squatters for each assigned worker
the sale of Crown land at a 'sufficient price'
questions.explanation: Wakefield argued that Crown land should be sold at a price high enough to stop labourers becoming landowners too quickly, with the proceeds used to bring out free emigrants. The scheme was meant to replace convict labour, not to tax it.

questions.stem: Many Chinese who came to the Victorian goldfields in the 1850s came from Guangdong province in southern China. Which conditions helped push them to emigrate?
options: Government land grants offered to families who settled overseas
The Meiji government's official encouragement of emigration to the Pacific
Poverty, pressure on land and the upheaval of the Taiping Rebellion
A famine caused by potato blight and mass evictions by landlords
questions.explanation: Southern China in the mid-19th century suffered rural poverty, natural disasters and the violence of the Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864), while news of gold offered a way to support families at home. The Meiji government ruled Japan, not China, and only from 1868.

questions.stem: Many Chinese gold-seekers travelled to Victoria under the 'credit-ticket' system. This meant that:
options: the British government paid their whole fare because they were imperial subjects
they bought a ticket that included a licence to mine on any goldfield
a merchant or broker advanced their fare, which they repaid from their earnings
the colonial government paid their fare in return for road-building work
questions.explanation: Under the credit-ticket system a merchant or broker paid the passage and the migrant repaid the debt, often through kin and district networks. Colonial governments did not fund Chinese passages; they taxed Chinese arrivals instead.

questions.stem: Caroline Chisholm is best known in colonial migration history for:
options: founding the Female Factory that housed and employed convict women at Parramatta
petitioning the Victorian parliament for women's right to vote
helping families and single women emigrate and find work in the colonies
leading the campaign to end transportation to Van Diemen's Land
questions.explanation: Chisholm ran a home for female immigrants in Sydney, found them employment and in 1849 founded the Family Colonization Loan Society to lend families the cost of passage. The Parramatta Female Factory predated her work and was a government institution.

questions.stem: In 1835 John Batman claimed to have bought land around Port Phillip from Wurundjeri elders. Governor Bourke's response was to:
options: send troops to remove all of Batman's party from Port Phillip
refer the agreement to London, where the Colonial Office ratified it
declare the agreement void, as only the Crown could dispose of the land
approve the agreement on condition that the Wurundjeri were paid rent each year
questions.explanation: Bourke's proclamation of 1835 declared the 'treaty' void and treated anyone occupying the land without Crown authority as a trespasser. Settlement was not reversed; the government soon took control of the district and sold the land itself.

questions.stem: Historians often describe Bourke's 1835 proclamation as a practical application of terra nullius. The main reason is that it:
options: created reserves on which the Kulin nations kept ownership of their Country
treated the land as Crown property that its Aboriginal owners had no right to sell
recognised Kulin ownership of the land but restricted its sale to the colonial government
ended pastoral occupation of the district until a treaty could be negotiated
questions.explanation: By voiding Batman's agreement on the grounds that only the Crown could dispose of the land, the proclamation denied that the Kulin peoples held any title to sell. It did not recognise Kulin ownership in any form, which is why it is linked to terra nullius.

questions.stem: Some historians argue that the Wurundjeri elders who met Batman in 1835 may have understood the exchange as a 'tanderrum' ceremony. If so, the elders were most likely:
options: granting visitors temporary access to Country and its resources
selling their land permanently in return for blankets and tools
accepting British sovereignty in exchange for official protection
declaring that Batman's party were trespassers who must leave
questions.explanation: Tanderrum was a ceremony that gave visitors safe passage and use of Country's resources for a time; it did not transfer the land. This reading suggests the two sides understood the meeting very differently, which is why the 'sale' is contested.

questions.stem: George Augustus Robinson became Chief Protector of Aborigines for the Port Phillip District in 1839. The Protectorate was set up largely because of:
options: conflict between Aboriginal people and the gold-seekers who flooded into the district
humanitarian concern in Britain, after a parliamentary inquiry, about violence on the frontier
squatters' demands that the colonial government remove Aboriginal people from their pastoral runs
a treaty with the Kulin nations that required the colony to appoint official protectors
questions.explanation: A House of Commons select committee on Aborigines in British settlements (1837) recommended protectors, and the Colonial Office established the Port Phillip Protectorate. Gold was not discovered in Victoria until 1851, after the Protectorate had ended.

questions.stem: Many of the squatters who took up runs in the Port Phillip District in the late 1830s had:
options: been granted land free as a reward for military service in India
arrived as assisted migrants under the Earl Grey orphan scheme
overlanded stock from New South Wales or shipped it from Van Diemen's Land
bought their runs at public auction from the officials of the Port Phillip Protectorate
questions.explanation: Pastoralists from Van Diemen's Land crossed Bass Strait, and overlanders drove sheep and cattle south from New South Wales, occupying Kulin and other Countries without purchase. The Earl Grey scheme brought orphan girls from 1848, not squatters.

questions.stem: What was the most immediate demographic effect of the gold discoveries of 1851 on Victoria?
options: Its population grew rapidly as people arrived from Britain, Europe, America and China
Its population fell as men left for the richer goldfields of New South Wales
Most new arrivals were convicts sent on from Van Diemen's Land to work the mines
Its population grew only slowly because the colony banned miners from foreign countries
questions.explanation: Victoria's population multiplied within a decade as gold-seekers arrived from around the world. Some people did leave for the New South Wales fields at first, but the Victorian discoveries soon drew far more people in.

questions.stem: Victoria's 1855 Act to restrict Chinese immigration imposed:
options: a dictation test in a European language for every Chinese arrival
a rule that each Chinese arrival must be employed by a pastoralist
a tax of 10 pounds on each Chinese arrival and a limit on Chinese passengers per ship
a ban on any Chinese miner holding a miner's right or a claim on a Victorian goldfield
questions.explanation: The 1855 Act charged a landing tax of 10 pounds for each Chinese passenger and limited the number of Chinese a ship could carry according to its tonnage. The dictation test came much later, with the Immigration Restriction Act 1901.

questions.stem: After 1855 thousands of Chinese gold-seekers landed at Robe in South Australia and walked hundreds of kilometres to the Victorian goldfields. They did this mainly to:
options: escape quarantine rules introduced at Melbourne for Asian ships
avoid Victoria's landing tax by arriving in a colony that had none
reach the central goldfields faster than by sailing through Port Phillip
join Chinese communities already well established in Adelaide
questions.explanation: South Australia did not tax Chinese arrivals at the time, so ships landed passengers at Robe and they travelled overland into Victoria. The long walk was slower and harder than landing at Melbourne, which shows the deterrent effect of the tax.

questions.stem: The Lambing Flat riots of 1860–61, in which European miners attacked Chinese miners, led most directly to:
options: the creation of separate Chinese Protectorates on the New South Wales goldfields
an intercolonial agreement that admitted Chinese miners on equal terms
the colony of New South Wales granting Chinese miners the right to vote
New South Wales passing its own law to restrict Chinese immigration in 1861
questions.explanation: After the riots New South Wales passed the Chinese Immigration Regulation and Restriction Act 1861, following Victoria's example. The Chinese Protectorate system belonged to Victoria, not New South Wales.

questions.stem: In 1879 Lowe Kong Meng, Cheok Hong Cheong and Louis Ah Mouy published 'The Chinese Question in Australia'. In it they:
options: urged the Qing government to withdraw all Chinese workers and merchants from the colonies
supported limits on Chinese labourers to protect the standing of merchants
demanded separate Chinese courts and self-government on the goldfields
argued against anti-Chinese laws, appealing to treaties and British ideals of justice
questions.explanation: The three Melbourne community leaders argued that discriminatory laws were unjust and inconsistent with the treaties that let British subjects live and trade in China. Their pamphlet is a key source for Chinese migrants' own perspectives.

questions.stem: In 1888 Chinese passengers on the steamer Afghan were refused permission to land in Melbourne and then Sydney, and an intercolonial conference on Chinese immigration followed. The episode is significant mainly because it showed:
options: the colonies agreeing at the conference to end all non-British immigration
Chinese merchants winning exemptions from every colonial restriction
the colonies coordinating Chinese exclusion more than a decade before Federation
the British government forcing the reluctant colonies to admit more Chinese migrants
questions.explanation: The 1888 conference agreed that the colonies should adopt uniform, tougher restrictions on Chinese immigration, a forerunner of the national policy of 1901. Britain was uneasy about the treatment of Chinese arrivals, but it did not force the colonies to admit them.

questions.stem: 'Booster literature' about the Australian colonies was:
options: religious tracts urging emigrants to work as missionaries
promotional writing that encouraged emigration by stressing opportunity
official reports warning British readers about violence on the frontier
newspapers published by gold miners to demand political reform
questions.explanation: Booster literature included guidebooks, pamphlets and lectures that promoted the colonies as healthy and prosperous, often exaggerating the ease of success. It was written to attract migrants, which affects its reliability as evidence.

questions.stem: A historian compares an emigration pamphlet describing Victoria as a 'land of plenty' with a shepherd's letters home in the 1850s describing loneliness, debt and harsh work. The most valid conclusion is that:
options: the pamphlet was written to attract migrants, so the letters may better reveal individual experience
the letters are unreliable because private writers always exaggerate their own hardships
the pamphlet is more reliable because it was printed and read by a larger audience
the two sources cannot be used together because they disagree about colonial life
questions.explanation: Purpose shapes content: promotional material had a reason to stress success, while private letters record one person's circumstances. Sources that disagree can still be used together; comparing them is how historians test each one.

questions.stem: Letters home from successful settlers often encouraged 'chain migration'. This means that:
options: migrants moved in stages from one colony to the next, following news of work
convicts were joined later by their families under government schemes
migrants were bound to employers through a series of labour contracts
relatives and neighbours followed earlier migrants, often to the same district
questions.explanation: Chain migration happened when news, money or sponsorship from earlier migrants drew family and community members after them. It helps explain why particular districts drew people from the same county or village.

questions.stem: In 1849 the ship Randolph, carrying convict exiles, was turned away from Port Phillip and sent on to Sydney. This reflects:
options: opposition from many free settlers who believed convict labour lowered wages and morals
squatters refusing to employ convicts because they preferred indentured Chinese workers
a ruling by the Legislative Council that exiles were already legally free settlers
the Kulin nations' demand that no further convicts be landed on their Country
questions.explanation: Public meetings in Melbourne opposed the landing, and Superintendent La Trobe sent the ship on. Many free settlers saw convicts as cheap competition and a moral 'stain'; the anti-transportation movement grew from these views.

questions.stem: In the 1840s many pastoralists supported renewed transportation or indentured Asian labour, while many urban free settlers opposed both. The best explanation for this division is that:
options: pastoralists opposed British rule, while urban settlers wished to remain loyal
urban settlers wanted more migrants, while pastoralists wanted a smaller population
pastoralists were mainly Irish Catholics, while urban settlers were mainly Protestants
pastoralists wanted cheap, controllable labour, while urban workers feared lower wages
questions.explanation: Squatters needed shepherds and labourers on remote runs and favoured any cheap supply, while urban workers and tradesmen saw convict or indentured labour as a threat to wages. The split was economic, not about loyalty to Britain.

questions.stem: Colonial governments in the 19th century assisted many single young women to migrate, often to work as domestic servants. A major reason was that:
options: British law barred single women from working in factories, mills or on farms
women were needed to replace assigned convicts as shepherds on runs
the Earl Grey scheme required equal numbers of orphan boys and girls
the colonies had far more men than women and wanted workers and future wives
questions.explanation: The colonial population was heavily male, and governments wanted domestic labour and stable families. The Earl Grey scheme (1848–1850) brought orphan girls only, mainly from Irish workhouses.

questions.stem: The Aboriginal Protection Act 1869 (Victoria) established:
options: a Board for the Protection of Aborigines with wide powers over Aboriginal lives
a system of land grants that returned Country to each Aboriginal clan
a special court to hear Aboriginal claims of frontier violence against settlers
a seat in parliament to be elected by Aboriginal men on each station
questions.explanation: The 1869 Act gave a statutory Board the power to control many aspects of Aboriginal people's lives. It did not return land; reserves remained Crown land that could be, and later was, taken back.

questions.stem: Under the 1869 Act and the regulations made under it, the Victorian government could:
options: pay compensation to clans for land taken by squatters before 1851
decide where Aboriginal people lived, control their work and remove their children
grant Aboriginal families freehold title to the land of stations such as Framlingham
allow Aboriginal men on stations to vote in Legislative Assembly elections
questions.explanation: The Act allowed the Governor to prescribe where Aboriginal people resided, to control their employment and earnings, and to provide for the custody of their children, which permitted removals. Station land stayed under government control rather than Aboriginal title.

questions.stem: The Aborigines Protection Act 1886 (Victoria), often called the 'Half-caste Act', required:
options: all Aboriginal people in Victoria to move onto one reserve at Lake Tyers
Aboriginal people of mixed descent to be counted as Europeans in the census
station managers to be elected each year by Aboriginal residents
many Aboriginal people of mixed descent to leave the stations and reserves
questions.explanation: The 1886 Act narrowed who the Board defined as 'Aboriginal' and required most people of mixed descent under 35 to leave the stations and support themselves. The concentration of people at Lake Tyers came decades later.

questions.stem: Which consequence of the 1886 Act is best supported by historical evidence?
options: People of mixed descent gained equal wages and voting rights in Victoria
Stations grew as Aboriginal people from other colonies moved onto them
The Board's control over people remaining on the stations was abolished
Families were divided, and stations lost workers and became less viable
questions.explanation: Forcing younger people of mixed descent off the stations separated them from parents, children and Country, and took skilled workers away from farming communities. The Board's control over those who remained continued and in some ways grew.

questions.stem: The 1886 Act reflected an assumption common among colonial officials that:
options: Aboriginal people should receive land as compensation for dispossession
Aboriginal people were entitled to the same rights as other British subjects
people of mixed descent should be absorbed into the settler population
Aboriginal culture would survive best on independent, self-governing reserves
questions.explanation: Officials expected people of mixed descent to 'merge' into the wider population while the Aboriginal population on stations declined, so the stations could eventually close. This early form of assimilation thinking ignored Aboriginal identity and kinship.

questions.stem: In colonial Australia, 'sectarianism' referred mainly to:
options: hostility between squatters and selectors over land
prejudice and rivalry between Protestants and Catholics
conflict between free settlers and emancipated convicts
rivalry between the colonies over tariffs and borders
questions.explanation: Sectarian division between a largely Protestant establishment and a largely Irish Catholic minority shaped politics, schooling and attitudes to Irish migration. The other conflicts were real, but they were not sectarian.

questions.stem: In the late 19th century many colonists believed in a hierarchy of races, sometimes justified as 'social Darwinism'. These ideas were used to argue that:
options: all races were equal and should be admitted to the colonies on the same terms
migrants should be chosen by their wealth and skills rather than their origins
Aboriginal people should hold land rights equal to those of the colonists
Aboriginal people were a 'dying race' and Asian migrants a threat to white society
questions.explanation: Racial hierarchy thinking cast Aboriginal decline as natural and inevitable, hiding the effects of dispossession and violence, and portrayed Asian migrants as a danger to a 'white' society. It was the opposite of ideas of racial equality.

questions.stem: The labour movement strongly supported restricting Asian and Pacific Islander immigration in the 1890s. Its main argument was that:
options: migrants from Asia would refuse to pay colonial taxes or rates
cheap labour would undercut white workers' wages and conditions
Asian migrants would take over the pastoral industry from squatters
free trade required the colonies to keep their labour costs high
questions.explanation: Unions argued that employers would use low-paid Asian and Pacific Islander workers to drive down wages; this economic argument was combined with racial ideas about a 'white' working man's country. It was not a claim about the pastoral industry's ownership.

questions.stem: From the 1880s the Bulletin magazine was known for:
options: publishing the official reports of the Aborigines Protection Boards
promoting a nationalist, often republican and strongly anti-Chinese identity
defending free trade and Chinese immigration as duties of the empire
campaigning for the return of convict transportation to New South Wales
questions.explanation: The Bulletin, founded in 1880, championed a distinct Australian identity and was fiercely hostile to Chinese immigration; from 1908 its masthead read 'Australia for the White Man'. It shows how national identity and race were bound together.

questions.stem: Japan's defeat of Russia in 1905 strengthened which idea in the new Commonwealth?
options: A belief that Australia should withdraw from the British Empire
Fear that an Asian power could threaten Australia, reinforcing White Australia
Confidence that Britain no longer needed to keep a navy in the Pacific
Support for admitting Japanese migrants because Japan was Britain's ally
questions.explanation: A modern Asian power defeating a European one sharpened fears of invasion and of threats to Australian sovereignty, strengthening support for immigration restriction and defence. Japan's alliance with Britain made the government cautious in wording its laws, not more open to Japanese migrants.

questions.stem: The main mechanism of the Immigration Restriction Act 1901 was:
options: a dictation test of 50 words in any European language chosen by an officer
a ban on any person who had not been born within the British Empire or its dominions
a poll tax charged on every non-European person arriving by sea
a quota allowing only 100 arrivals from Asia in each year
questions.explanation: An officer could give an unwanted arrival a dictation test in a language they did not know, so the test was designed to be failed. Poll taxes had been the colonial method; the 1901 Act replaced them with the test.

questions.stem: The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 used a dictation test rather than an openly racial ban. The main reason was that:
options: the labour movement wanted skilled Asian workers to be able to enter the country
the new government wished to protect Chinese merchants already living in Australia
Britain objected to openly racial laws that could offend Japan and its Indian subjects
the High Court had ruled that racial bans on immigration were unconstitutional
questions.explanation: The Colonial Office urged a test modelled on Natal's that did not name race, to avoid offending Japan and British subjects in India. The High Court did not sit until 1903, so it could not have ruled on the law.

questions.stem: The Pacific Island Labourers Act 1901:
options: granted farmland to Pacific Islanders who had completed their indenture contracts
ended recruitment of Pacific Islanders and provided for most to be deported after 1906
gave Pacific Islanders working on sugar plantations the right to vote in elections
allowed Queensland planters to keep recruiting Pacific Islanders until the 1920s
questions.explanation: The Act stopped new recruitment after 1904 and provided for the deportation of most Pacific Islanders remaining after 1906, although some long-term residents were allowed to stay. Many had been recruited by deception or force, a practice known as blackbirding.

questions.stem: Many Queensland sugar planters opposed the end of Pacific Islander labour. The Commonwealth eased their opposition mainly by:
options: exempting Queensland from the Immigration Restriction Act
compensating planters for each labourer who was deported
paying a bounty on sugar grown and harvested by white labour
allowing planters to recruit indentured labourers from India instead
questions.explanation: An excise on sugar was combined with a bounty, later set by the Sugar Bounty Act 1903, for sugar produced with white labour, so the industry could survive without Pacific Islander workers. Recruiting labourers from India would have contradicted White Australia.

questions.stem: The Naturalisation Act 1903:
options: allowed Chinese residents to be naturalised after fifteen years of continuous residence
barred most people of Asian, African and Pacific Islander origin from naturalising
made every resident of the Commonwealth an Australian citizen from 1903
required naturalised migrants to pass a dictation test again every year
questions.explanation: The Act excluded people it called 'aboriginal natives' of Asia, Africa and the Pacific Islands (other than New Zealand) from naturalisation, which in turn shut them out of other rights. Australian citizenship did not exist until 1949.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth Maternity Allowance Act 1912:
options: provided free hospital care at birth for all women living in the Commonwealth
paid five pounds to mothers only if the child's father was a member of a union
paid five pounds on the birth of a child but excluded Aboriginal and Asian mothers
paid a weekly allowance only to married mothers who had been born in Britain
questions.explanation: The Fisher Labor government's payment was available to married and unmarried mothers, which was progressive for the time, but it excluded Aboriginal women and women from Asia and the Pacific Islands. It was a single payment, not a weekly allowance.

questions.stem: The Maternity Allowance was available to unmarried mothers but excluded Aboriginal and Asian mothers. This suggests that in the new nation the benefits of belonging were:
options: shared equally by all residents, whatever their race or marital status
left entirely to the states, which decided who would be included
tied to race and to building a white population, more than to marital status
defined by whether a mother was married rather than by her racial background
questions.explanation: Paying unmarried white mothers while excluding Aboriginal and Asian mothers shows that race, not respectability, was the deciding line. The payment was national, part of a pattern of early Commonwealth laws that linked welfare to whiteness.

questions.stem: As originally written, section 127 of the Constitution provided that:
options: Aboriginal people were declared British subjects without exception
Aboriginal people were not to be counted in reckoning the population
Aboriginal people could not vote in any Commonwealth election
the Commonwealth had the sole power to make laws for Aboriginal people
questions.explanation: Section 127 excluded 'aboriginal natives' from counts of the population used, for example, to share seats and revenue among the states. Voting rights were dealt with elsewhere, mainly by the Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902.

questions.stem: As originally written, the race power in section 51(xxvi) of the Constitution allowed the Commonwealth to make special laws for:
options: the people of any race other than the Aboriginal race in any State
Aboriginal people living in the federal territories, but not in the States
any group, provided the law did not discriminate by race
migrants from Britain who had not yet been naturalised
questions.explanation: The power was intended for laws about non-European groups such as Pacific Islanders and Indian or Chinese workers, while Aboriginal affairs were left to the states. Nothing in the original Constitution prohibited racial discrimination.

questions.stem: In 1901, the formal national status of people born in Australia was that they were:
options: British subjects, because Australian citizenship did not yet exist
Australian citizens, as defined in one of the sections of the Constitution
citizens only of the state in which they had been born
dual citizens of Australia and the United Kingdom
questions.explanation: Australians were British subjects until Australian citizenship was created from 26 January 1949. The Constitution does not define citizenship, so rights were shaped by laws such as those on voting, naturalisation and welfare.

questions.stem: In 'Drawing the Global Colour Line' (2008), Marilyn Lake and Henry Reynolds interpret White Australia as:
options: a policy imposed by the British government on unwilling colonies
part of a transnational movement to create 'white men's countries'
a uniquely Australian policy without parallels in other countries
mainly a temporary response to the economic depression of the 1890s
questions.explanation: Lake and Reynolds trace how ideas and laws of racial exclusion moved between Australia, the USA, Canada, New Zealand and South Africa. Their interpretation places White Australia in a global context rather than treating it as unique.

questions.stem: Which judgement about continuity and change from 1834 to 1913 is best supported by evidence?
options: Racial attitudes changed from exclusion in the 1850s to broad inclusion by 1913
Aboriginal people regained control of much of their land after Federation
Chinese migration rose steadily after 1901 as new goldfields opened
Migration diversified the population, yet laws increasingly defined belonging by race
questions.explanation: Gold-rush migration brought people from many nations, but colonial poll taxes, protection laws and the post-Federation Acts drew ever firmer racial lines around who belonged. Chinese numbers fell after 1901 under the dictation test.
